rebuttal.value:
Hello Reviewer c2H7,

Thank you for your positive score and feedback, particularly for recognizing our data collection effort by referring to DroneAudioSet as the ‘largest and most dimensionally comprehensive drone audio dataset to date‘ that ‘fills the gap in research on real-world drone acoustic interactions‘. Below, we address the concerns raised one-by-one. 
***

## C1. Accounting for Environment Reverberation and Multipath Effects
We perform experiments in three different indoor environments, by additionally varying the drone-to-source distance, in order to add diversity in terms of reverberation and multipath. However, we acknowledge that this alone is insufficient to represent the wide range of clutter and reflective / absorptive materials that may arise in real-world search and rescue settings. While we leave data collection in complex indoor / outdoor environments as future work, data augmentation methods based on synthetic room impulse responses (such as those proposed by Tang, Zhenyu, et al. “GWA: A large high-quality acoustic dataset for audio processing.” ACM SIGGRAPH 2022) can enable creation of a larger dataset with reverberation for model generalization. We will add this to Section 5 (Discussion) of our camera-ready version. 
***

## C2. Static Frame Limitation
We acknowledge the limitations of our static frame setup, which cannot replicate the micro-dynamics of a hovering use-case. As mentioned under Limitations and Future Work (in Section 5), our testbed gives us the flexibility of experimenting with 216 different configurations – a key advantage of a controlled data-collection setup, but at the expense of a realistic hovering scenario. That said, our controlled data collection design enables actionable insights, such as recommendations for microphone placement and drone throttle settings (see Section 4.2), that can inform the development of more realistic and dynamic hovering scenarios. We view our dataset as an important step towards realizing the full potential of audio in real-world drone-based search and rescue missions.
***

## C3. Standardizing Formatting Styles of Tables and Figures
We will make the following changes to the camera-ready version --
* Update Table 3 as well as Table 5 (in supplementary material) to have the same border style as the other tables (i.e., two horizontal lines between header row and the rest, and vertical lines to close the table at the left and right ends).
* Modify the plots in Figs. 2, 3 and 4 to have a similar color scheme. In particular, we will use a common color-blind friendly color palette. 
* Increase the font-size of the labels and legends in Figs. 3 and 4.

Hello Reviewer uS38,

Thank you for your positive feedback and score, for recognizing our dataset as a ‘solid test-bed for both algorithm research and hardware design’ which is ‘filling the gap of real drone-audio resources‘. The review points out a few limitations of our collected dataset, which we view as great candidates for future work. We elaborate on them below. 
***

## C1: Static Frame Limitation
We acknowledge the limitations of our static frame setup, which cannot replicate the micro-dynamics of a hovering use-case. As mentioned under Limitations and Future Work (in Section 5), our testbed gives us the flexibility of experimenting with 216 different configurations – a key advantage of a controlled data-collection setup, but at the expense of a realistic hovering scenario. That said, our controlled data collection design enables actionable insights, such as recommendations for microphone placement and drone throttle settings (see Section 4.2), that can inform the development of more realistic and dynamic hovering scenarios. We view our dataset as an important step towards realizing the full potential of audio in real-world drone-based search and rescue missions.
***

## C2: Non-Human Sounds Not Exploited for Disaster-Event Detection
While the focus of our paper is on detecting the human distress sounds for rescuing humans,    we agree that there is value in accurately detecting non-human sounds as well, during search and rescue, e.g., the characteristic of burning sounds to identify the source of fire. We will include this under Limitations and Future Work (in Section 5) of the camera-ready version. 
***

## C3: Extending to Outdoor Scenarios
In comparison to indoor settings, outdoor scenarios have a completely different acoustic environment (more wind noise as opposed to multipath and reverberations). In addition, the signal-to-noise ratio levels in outdoor environments will also likely be lower than indoors due to larger distances between the drone and the target humans. Overall, we agree that the addition of outdoor settings can add more diversity to our existing dataset. As mentioned in the review, we believe that the first step towards that can be to collect data from low risk flights in outdoor settings and synthetically augment target sounds. We will discuss this point on outdoor settings in Section 5 of our camera-ready version.

rebuttal.value:
Hello Reviewer xVsc,

Thank you for your strong score and positive review, especially for recognizing our dataset to be ‘very well distributed’ and a ‘unique contribution with a large diversity of conditions’, whose utility we demonstrate with ‘exemplary applications’. We are pleased that you found our paper ‘well-written’ with ‘sufficient technical details’. We will now respond to your concerns one-by-one. 
***

## C1: Figure Readability
Thank you for your detailed comments on how to improve Figs. 3 and 4. As suggested, we will make the following changes in the camera-ready version – increase the font size, remove unnecessary borders, expand the legend to the whole width of the image, reduce the width of the boxes in the box-plots, and make the phrasing concise (e.g., remove ‘configuration’ from the legend, and shorten x-axis label to ‘Mic Types’). We will also modify the color scheme to be consistent with other figures. 
***

## C2: “What are the brackets with stars?” (in Figs. 3 and 4)
The stars (*) indicate statistical significance in SI-SDR values (with p<0.05) between the two conditions represented by the brackets. We mentioned this in the footnote on Page 8, where we applied Shapiro-Wilk normality testing, followed by Tukey HSD (if normal distribution) or Wilcoxon signed-rank with Bonferroni correction (if non-normal). We will update the caption of Figs. 3 and 4 to also explain the annotations of statistical significance. 
***

## C3: Technical Details about Speakers and Microphones
We used a JBL Flip 6 speaker with a frequency response from 63Hz to 20kHz, and a Signal-to-Noise Ratio over 80dB, sufficient to replicate low, mid and high frequencies of human speech, screams and non-verbal cues, as well as ambient sounds (e.g., dripping water and burning fire). We will also clarify the microphone’s frequency response (60Hz to 20kHz) as pointed out in the review, and explicitly mention that the potential ultrasound frequency sounds of the rotors (beyond 20kHz) cannot be accurately captured. We will update these details in Section 3 of the camera-ready submission.   
***

## C4: Regarding Attaching Microphones and the UAV to a Common Frame
 The review mentions that ‘this dataset may be slightly harder than comparable situations in real life’ as the ‘microphones and the UAV is fixed to the same frame’. Thank you for your critical observation. While it is unclear what future deployments of microphones on drones would look like, we envision that the microphones will be connected to drones, either directly affixed or through a solid structure, both of which will involve mechanical coupling between the two, resulting in structural vibrations being captured by the microphones. Hence, we created a setup with a common frame between the two. In addition, throughout the recording sessions, we ensured that the drone remained securely and evenly attached to the frame to prevent any anomalous vibrations. We will clarify this in the paper.  
***

## C5: Updating the GitHub code
We will update our code to do the following two things during the camera-ready submission –
* Load the audio data directly from HuggingFace instead of assuming raw audio and text annotation files.
* Create a single script (instead of Jupyter notebook) that loads the data from HuggingFace, performs noise suppression as well as classification.

summary.value: This paper presents a dataset designed to train noise suppression methods to understand human voices and noises over UAV rotor noise. The use case is rescue operations in which drones are used to listen for humans. The authors fixed a number of microphones on an aluminium profile frame under and over different drones, which were also fixed in the frame. That way the authors varied controlled conditions, such as relative distance and position of microphones to the UAV and the drone's size and rotor speed. Human voices and signals from respective datasets were played from a sound source at a specific distance from the aluminum frame. The dataset provides different signal-to-noise ratios created with the varying parameters.

strengths_contributions.value:
The dataset seems to provide a unique contribution with a larger diversity of conditions than previous datasets and a significant size. Having individual audio samples of the signal and noise sources is also a useful addition. The dataset seems to provide some reverb diversity; the rooms in Figure 5 (appendix) seem to indicate highly reflective surfaces in one and carpeted surfaces in another room, used for data collection.

The paper is well written. It provides sufficient technical details to understand the recording conditions. Investigations into the Signal-to-Noise Ratios, shown in figure 2, are valuable to make sure the claimed diversity is actually in the data. 

The authors provide also exemplary applications, such as human presence detection, whose performance measures show intuitively unsurprising trends; clearer signals lead to higher performance. While the general conclusions of this part seem obvious it is good to have them evaluated in controlled settings. It is a good sanity check if the dataset can be used for the use case claimed.

Information about the recording environment in the supplementary complete this work.

The audio examples on the website give a good intuition that there are hard and easy examples in this dataset. As a human listening, the signal is sometimes easily recognizable and sometimes hidden. 

The dataset is very well distributed and supported by code and models at Github and Huggingface already. There is one issue with Huggingface (see further down) but I do not think the authors should be punished for it.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
There are some minor issues with the presentation. Figure 3 has quite small fonts, unneeded borders and a layout that seems unpolished. Please increase font size, consider removing borders and try to improve overall design. The legend takes up quite some space, maybe the legend title, e.g. Configuration, could be removed and high throttle and low throttle could be abbreviated so that the legend is so small that it fits as hovering over the figure. Same for Microphone Distance. Also, what are the brackets with stars?

The hardware of the speaker should be included. From the pictures it seems a JBL speaker was used. This one has a limited frequency spectrum and specific response. Data about technical data of the speaker should be added to the supplementary material. The microphone seems to be able to detect 60 Hz to 20 kHz. The speaker can probably reproduce sounds in a similar spectrum. The rotors emit potentially some ultrasound noise which can not be captured with those microphones. These insights may be useful for researchers developing noise suppression algorithms. The frequency spectrum of the speaker informs about the difference to real world recordings. Limitations of the microphone make ultrasound-based work impossible. This is not necessarily a negative point but a request to be explicit about these technical information.

One potential issue could be that microphones and the UAV is fixed to the same frame. There can be vibrations traveling along the rigid aluminium frame which can increase the noise. However, that means that this dataset may be slightly harder than comparable situations in real life but still the classification results show the task is not impossible and as a human listening to the examples, rotor noise and faint human sounds over rotor noise sound plausible and not too disturbed by potential frame vibrations. If the authors did any investigation into the issue of vibration traveling along the frame it could be good commenting on it in the paper.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: "If you identified no concerns (selected the 'No' option): clearly explain why no significant ethical concerns remain" - I apologize but this review request in the form does not make sense to me. If there are no ethical concerns there are no ethical concerns. Seeing the possible ethics flags in the review form I conclude the presented work poses no ethical issues regarding any of those categories apart from the potential of crashing drones who search for humans which may have a negative environmental impact.

dataset_code_comments.value: Unfortunately Huggingface converted the whole dataset into parquet files which makes it easier to process the data for Hugging Face. After the final upload from the authors (the date can be tracked) it can be seen that one day later a bot went over the data for conversion. This was probably not anticipated by the authors. In 5 min I was able to load and inspect the data with 2 lines of python code so I do not think this is a major concern. However, the code provided on the webpage does seem to work with the raw data in wav and txt files so a conversion needs to happen or the code on Github needs to be re-written. This is a minor problem and can be solved in a few days ahead of the camera ready deadline. It is still possible to access the whole dataset and inspect it which I did for selected samples.

additional_feedback.value: This is neither a positive or negative point but I would prefer one easy script which does the classification task on the data instead of one very very large jupyter notebook. For the purpose of inspecting the data and verifying core functionalities the jupyter notebook works but as a question of preference I would suggest adding one simple python script that loads the data, maybe trains a classification and outputs results.

final_justification.value: The authors responded adequately to my biggest concern, having the microphones connected via a static frame. There seem to be no points raised by other reviewers that would downgrade my rating so I keep it at accept.

summary.value: This study releases DroneAudioSet—the first real-world audio dataset explicitly designed for drone-based search-and-rescue. It provides 23.5 h of annotated recordings that span extreme SNR conditions from 60 dB to 0 dB. The corpus systematically combines 2 drone platforms, 17 microphone layouts, three source categories (human-vocal, human-non-vocal, and ambient), and three indoor venues, capturing the acoustics of each configuration. Benchmark experiments show that state-of-the-art noise-suppression and classification pipelines break down at very low SNR, especially for non-vocal human sounds whose F1 drops to ≈ 0.2. Empirical analysis yields concrete hardware guidelines: “over-drone microphone array + 50 cm suspension” and “small drone at low throttle” maximise SI-SDR, furnishing an engineering recipe while filling the gap of real drone-audio resources.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Key gap filled – The first real dataset that reaches the extreme –60 dB SNR regime, far beyond previous work (e.g., DREGON only ≈ –16 dB).

2. Systematic variable control – Microphone position/distance, throttle, and source type are all factorised, giving a solid test-bed for both algorithm research and hardware design; the paper distils an optimal mic-layout scheme that can be applied in practice.

3. Data scale & diversity – 23.5 h greatly exceeds prior sets (DREGON 6.12 h) and covers multiple rooms and sound sources (baby cries, claps, fire crackle, etc.).

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Static-frame limitation: The rigid mounting frame cannot replicate the micro-dynamics of true hovering (e.g., balance corrections that alter the acoustic field). It is suggested to add a small number of free-hover recordings or augment the data with fluid-simulation noise profiles.

2. Untapped non-human (NH) potential: Non-human (NH) sounds are treated only as interference; the dataset is not yet exploited for disaster-event detection. It is suggested that a sub-task be introduced that identifies critical NH events after denoising and analyzes the intelligibility of NH classes.

3. Current release is indoor-only, the acquisition framework (multi-mic rigs, calibrated SNR labels) is scalable. Extending to outdoor scenarios—starting with low-risk flights and synthetic augmentation—would substantially increase the dataset’s utility for real deployments.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The authors supply fully documented, publicly hosted data and executable code, with detailed experimental configs that jointly ensure straightforward access and complete reproducibility.

final_justification.value: Overall, I believe this paper is ready for acceptance. I am also satisfied with the authors' responses. I will maintain my initial score.

summary.value: This study presents DRONEAUDIOSET, the first public audio dataset for drone-based search and rescue scenarios. It contains 23.5 hours of multi-dimensional annotated recordings, covering SNR from -60 dB to 0 dB, different drone types, throttle settings, microphone configurations, and environments. Through systematic evaluation of noise suppression and classification models, the study reveals the limitations of existing methods under extreme low-SNR conditions and provides practical design recommendations for microphone placement and drone throttle adjustment based on experimental analyses. The dataset fills the gap in research on real-world drone acoustic interactions, serving as a crucial benchmark for developing related algorithms and system designs.

strengths_contributions.value:
1 Constructs the largest and most dimensionally comprehensive drone audio dataset to date, covering key variables such as SNR, drone types, and environments.  
2 Employs a controlled experimental design for data collection, providing a standardized benchmark for follow-up research.  
3 Conducts multi-SNR group comparisons of traditional, neural, and hybrid noise suppression methods, quantifying performance degradation of different approaches under extreme noise, especially the limitations in non-human sound classification.  
4 Proposes microphone placement strategies and throttle adjustment recommendations that directly link drone hardware design to SAR mission requirements, offering clear engineering guidance.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1 Experiments are conducted only in indoor environments, excluding complex outdoor scenarios. Factors such as environmental reverberation and multipath effects in real SAR operations may affect model generalization.  
2 Drones are fixed on a frame to simulate hovering, without considering the dynamic impacts of fuselage vibration and airflow changes during flight on noise characteristics.  
3 It is recommended that the authors standardize the formatting style of tables and figures in the paper.

title.value: DroneAudioset: An Audio Dataset for Drone-based Search and Rescue

TLDR.value: We develop "DroneAudioset", a dataset that provides audio recordings from drone-mounted microphones to inform noise suppression and sound classification techniques for drone-audition based human presence detection in search and rescue missions.

abstract.value:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) or drones, are increasingly used in search and rescue missions to detect human presence. Existing systems primarily leverage vision-based methods which are prone to fail under low-visibility or occlusion. Drone-based audio perception offers promise but suffers from extreme ego-noise that masks sounds indicating human presence.  
Existing datasets are either limited in diversity or synthetic, lacking real acoustic interactions, and there are no standardized setups for drone audition. To this end, we present DroneAudioset (The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ahlab-drone-project/DroneAudioSet/ under the MIT license), a comprehensive drone audition dataset featuring 23.5 hours of annotated recordings, covering a wide range of signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) from -57.2 dB to -2.5 dB, across various drone types, throttles, microphone configurations as well as environments. The dataset enables development and systematic evaluation of noise suppression and classification methods for human-presence detection under challenging conditions, while also informing practical design considerations for drone audition systems, such as microphone placement trade-offs, and development of drone noise-aware audio processing. This dataset is an important step towards enabling design and deployment of drone-audition systems.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
